lessons.title: An Inspector Calls: context
lessons.summary: Understand the two worlds behind the play, Edwardian 1912 and post-war 1945, learn about Priestley's life and politics, and practise using context to strengthen AO3 answers.
objectives: I can explain why Priestley set the play in 1912 but wrote it in 1945.
I can describe the class system, working conditions and position of women in Edwardian Britain.
I can outline Priestley's experiences and socialist beliefs and link them to the play.
I can explain how a 1945 audience would have responded to the play's message.
I can integrate context into analysis instead of adding it as a separate fact.

activities.title: Two dates: 1912 and 1945
activities.content:
## A play with a double context

*An Inspector Calls* is set in **spring 1912** but was written in **1945**, in the final months of the Second World War. Priestley chose the gap on purpose, and the whole play depends on it.

**1912** was the high point of Edwardian confidence. Britain ruled a huge empire, industry was booming, and wealthy families like the Birlings believed the good times would last. But beneath the surface were serious tensions: strikes, poverty, the campaign for women's votes, and growing rivalry with Germany.

**Between the two dates** the audience had lived through the First World War (1914–18), the General Strike of 1926, the Great Depression of the 1930s, and the Second World War (1939–45). Every one of Birling's confident predictions had been proved wrong.

**1945** was a moment of decision. The war was ending, cities were bombed, and people wanted a fairer society. In July 1945 the country voted in a Labour government promising a welfare state: free healthcare, better housing and support for the unemployed.

Priestley uses the gap between the dates to create **dramatic irony**. The audience watches the Birlings with the knowledge of what is coming, so their smugness looks foolish and their selfishness looks dangerous. The play asks the 1945 audience: will you build the world Birling wanted, or the one the Inspector describes?

activities.title: Using the double context in a paragraph
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Priestley use Birling to criticise the attitudes of his time?

> Priestley sets Birling up as the voice of Edwardian confidence and then lets history knock him down. In Act One, Birling dismisses the idea of war with Germany and holds up the newest ocean liner as proof of unstoppable progress. For the audience of 1945, who had survived two world wars and knew the fate of that ship, every prediction is a small explosion of dramatic irony. Priestley does not need the Inspector to tell us Birling is wrong; the audience's own memories do it. This matters because Birling's views about war and progress are bundled together with his views about workers and responsibility. By discrediting the first, Priestley undermines the second, so that when the Inspector arrives the audience is already prepared to reject the belief that a man should look after only himself.

**What earns AO3 marks here:** the paragraph uses both dates, explains **why** the gap matters, and links context directly to a **dramatic method** and to **Priestley's purpose**.

question.text: Why did Priestley set his 1945 play in 1912?
question.hint: Think about what the audience knew that the characters did not.
question.explanation: Setting the play in 1912 lets the audience watch Birling's confident predictions in the knowledge that they all failed. This dramatic irony discredits Birling and warns the 1945 audience not to return to the attitudes that led to war and inequality.

options.text: So the audience's knowledge of the two world wars would expose the Birlings' confidence as foolish and dangerous
Because Priestley was born in 1912 and wanted to write about his childhood
Because police inspectors were only introduced in 1912
Because theatres in 1945 were not allowed to show contemporary plays

activities.title: Edwardian Britain: class, work and women
activities.content:
## The world of the Birlings

**Class.** Edwardian society was a strict hierarchy. At the top were the aristocracy, families like the Crofts with titles and land. Below them, wealthy industrialists like Birling, who had money but not breeding, and who badly wanted to marry into the class above. Beneath them, a small middle class of clerks and shopkeepers, and then the vast working class. Around a third of the population lived in poverty.

**Work.** There was no minimum wage, no unemployment benefit and no legal protection from being sacked. Workers who organised strikes, as Eva does, could be dismissed and blacklisted. In 1912 alone there were major strikes by miners and dock workers, so Birling's fear of trouble from workers was widely shared by employers.

**Women.** Women could not vote in national elections until 1918, and then only if they were over 30 and met a property qualification. Working-class women had the lowest-paid jobs and no protection from harassment. An unmarried pregnant woman faced disgrace and could expect no help from the state; charities like Mrs Birling's committee were often the only option, and they judged who was deserving.

**No welfare state.** Everything Priestley's audience would soon take for granted, such as free healthcare and benefits, did not exist. Eva's death in the infirmary, poor and alone, was an ordinary tragedy of the time. That is precisely why Priestley chose it.

question.text: Match each feature of Edwardian Britain to the part of the play it helps explain.
question.hint: Think about strikes, charities, marriage between classes, and the lack of any state support.
question.explanation: Birling sacks Eva after a strike because employers could dismiss workers freely. Mrs Birling's committee shows how charity replaced state welfare. Birling's eagerness about the engagement reflects the desire to marry into the aristocracy. Eva's lonely death reflects the absence of a welfare state.

pairs.left: Employers could sack striking workers without penalty
pairs.right: Birling dismisses Eva for leading a demand for higher wages

pairs.left: Charities decided who was 'deserving' of help
pairs.right: Mrs Birling's committee refuses Eva support

pairs.left: Industrialists wanted to marry into the aristocracy
pairs.right: Birling is delighted about Sheila's engagement to a Croft

pairs.left: There was no welfare state or free healthcare
pairs.right: Eva dies poor and alone in the infirmary

activities.title: Priestley: his life and beliefs
activities.content:
## Who was J. B. Priestley?

**Early life.** Priestley was born in Bradford in 1894, the son of a schoolteacher. He grew up in a northern industrial town very like Brumley, among mill workers and their families, and left school at sixteen to work as a clerk.

**The First World War.** He volunteered in 1914 and served in the trenches, where he was wounded and gassed. Most of his friends were killed. He blamed the older generation of leaders for sending the young to die, a bitterness that shapes the play's contrast between the generations.

**The Second World War.** Priestley became one of the most popular voices in Britain through his radio broadcasts in 1940, listened to by millions. He argued that the war should lead to a fairer, more equal country. His broadcasts were eventually taken off the air, partly because some politicians thought them too left-wing.

**Politics.** Priestley was a **socialist**. He believed that wealth and power should be shared more fairly, that the community had a duty to look after its weakest members, and that capitalism unchecked led to exploitation. In 1942 he helped found a political party pushing for these ideas, and he campaigned for the reforms that produced the welfare state.

**The play.** He wrote *An Inspector Calls* in a matter of weeks in 1945. Its first performances were in Moscow that year; London saw it in 1946. The Inspector's speech about one body and shared responsibility is Priestley's own creed, dramatised.

question.text: Complete the sentences about Priestley's life.

metadata.blanksText: Priestley was born in the industrial town of ___ in 1894. He fought in the trenches during the ___ World War. His political beliefs are best described as ___.

question.hint: A Yorkshire city; the war that began in 1914; a belief in shared wealth and community.
question.explanation: Priestley grew up in Bradford, served in the First World War, and was a committed socialist who argued for a fairer post-war society.

activities.title: Specific references and dramatic traditions
activities.content:
## Details the audience would catch

**The unsinkable ship.** Birling praises a new liner about to sail. The audience knew it as the Titanic, which sank in April 1912 on its first voyage, weeks after the play's setting. It becomes a symbol of arrogant confidence heading for disaster, exactly Birling's position.

**No war.** Birling insists the Germans do not want war. Within two years Britain was at war. The Inspector's warning about fire, blood and anguish would have sounded, to a 1945 audience, like a description of what actually happened, twice.

**Strikes.** Birling expects labour trouble to blow over. The following decades brought the largest strikes in British history.

**Capital and labour.** Birling and Croft are business rivals hoping to merge. The play shows the wealthy uniting to protect profits while workers like Eva are dismissed for asking for a few shillings more.

## Dramatic traditions

- **The well-made play**: a popular form with secrets, tension and a neat ending. Priestley borrows its shape and then breaks it with the final phone call.
- **The morality play**: medieval dramas in which characters representing vices are confronted and taught a lesson. The Birlings each embody a failing (greed, pride, lust, envy) and the Inspector acts like the voice of judgement.
- **The detective story**: a whodunnit in which everyone did it.

Priestley combines familiar forms so that a radical message reaches a mainstream audience.

activities.title: Bolt-on versus integrated context
activities.content:
AO3 rewards context that **explains** a choice in the text. Compare these two attempts at the same point about Mrs Birling.

**Bolt-on (weak):**
> In 1912 there was no welfare state and charities helped the poor. Mrs Birling is on a charity committee and she refuses to help Eva. This shows she is cruel.

**Integrated (strong):**
> Because there was no welfare state in 1912, organisations like Mrs Birling's committee were often the last hope for a pregnant, unmarried woman. Priestley gives Mrs Birling this power precisely so that the audience sees how charity controlled by the wealthy could become a tool of judgement rather than help. Her refusal is not simply personal cruelty; it reflects a system in which the rich decided who deserved to survive. For an audience in 1945, about to vote on whether the state should guarantee support for all, the scene is an argument for replacing private charity with public responsibility.

**Differences:**
- The strong version says **why Priestley chose** this detail.
- It moves from the individual to the **system**.
- It ends with the **1945 audience**, connecting both contexts.

question.text: True or false: the play was first performed in Britain before the end of the Second World War.
question.hint: Think about where the first performances took place and when London audiences saw it.
question.explanation: False. Although it was written in 1945, the first performances were in Moscow that year, and the London premiere came in 1946, after the war had ended and the Labour government had been elected.

options.text: True
False

question.text: Explain how an audience in 1945 or 1946 might have responded to the Inspector's warning that people who do not learn responsibility will be taught it in fire, blood and anguish.
question.hint: What had the audience just lived through? What were they about to decide about the future of the country?
question.explanation: The audience had lived through two world wars, so the warning would sound like a description of their own recent experience, giving the Inspector enormous authority. Many would connect it to the 1945 election and the promise of a welfare state, hearing the speech as a call to build a fairer society. Priestley thus uses the audience's memories to make the Inspector's message urgent rather than abstract.

markScheme.criterion: Links the warning to the audience's recent experience of one or both world wars
Explains that this experience gives the Inspector's words authority or makes them feel true or prophetic
Connects the message to the 1945 election, the welfare state, or the chance to build a fairer society

question.text:
How does Priestley use the context of 1912 and 1945 to present his ideas in An Inspector Calls? Write about:

- how Priestley presents the society of 1912 through the Birlings
- how the play's message relates to the audience of 1945.
question.hint: Cover class and the position of workers and women in 1912, Birling's predictions and dramatic irony, Priestley's socialism and war experience, and the 1945 election and welfare state.
question.explanation: A strong answer describes Edwardian class divisions, the lack of welfare and the vulnerability of working women as shown through Eva and the Birlings; explains Birling's failed predictions as dramatic irony; connects the Inspector's message to Priestley's socialism and war experience; and shows how the 1945 audience, voting for a welfare state, were invited to reject the Birlings' world.

markScheme.criterion: Describes the Edwardian class system or the gap between rich and poor as shown through the Birlings and Eva
Refers to the position of workers or women in 1912 (strikes, no rights, no vote, no welfare)
Explains Birling's mistaken predictions as dramatic irony that discredits his views
Links the Inspector's message to Priestley's socialism or his experiences of war
Relates the play to the 1945 audience, the election or the welfare state
Explains Priestley's purpose: persuading the audience to reject the Birlings' values and choose a fairer society

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Set in **1912**, written in **1945**: the gap creates **dramatic irony** as the audience knows Birling's predictions fail.
- **Edwardian Britain**: rigid class system, no welfare state, workers sacked for striking, women without votes or protection, charities deciding who was deserving.
- **Priestley**: Bradford-born, fought in the First World War, famous wartime broadcaster, committed **socialist** who campaigned for a fairer post-war society.
- **1945**: war ending, Labour elected, welfare state coming; the Inspector's speech is Priestley's argument for that future.
- Specific references: the **Titanic**, **no war**, **strikes**, business mergers.
- Forms borrowed: **well-made play**, **morality play**, **detective story**.
- For AO3, explain **why Priestley chose** a detail and connect **both** contexts to his purpose.

practiceQuestions.text: In which year was An Inspector Calls written?
practiceQuestions.hint: The Second World War was ending.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Priestley wrote the play in 1945, setting it in 1912 to exploit the audience's knowledge of everything that had happened in between.

options.feedback: 1912 is the year in which the play is set.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: in 1912 there was a welfare state providing free healthcare and unemployment benefit for everyone.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about why Eva had to go to a charity committee.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. There was no comprehensive welfare state in 1912; the poor depended on charity, family or the workhouse. The welfare state was created after 1945.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which event does Birling's praise of the new 'unsinkable' liner point towards?
practiceQuestions.hint: It sank in April 1912 on its first voyage.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birling is describing the Titanic, which sank on its maiden voyage in April 1912. The audience's knowledge of this makes his confidence look foolish.

options.text: The sinking of the Titanic
The outbreak of the Second World War
The General Strike of 1926
The Labour victory of 1945

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of these facts about Priestley's life are most relevant to the play's message?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what shaped his views on the older generation and on sharing wealth.
practiceQuestions.explanation: His service in the First World War made him bitter about the older generation's leadership, and his socialism drives the Inspector's message. His birthplace and later travels are less directly connected to the play's argument.

options.text: He fought in the trenches and blamed older leaders for the deaths of the young
He was a socialist who campaigned for a fairer post-war society
He wrote travel books about America
He was born in the same year as Sheila Birling

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about the 1945 context.

metadata.blanksText: In July 1945 the ___ Party won a landslide election victory, promising to build a ___ state that would provide healthcare and support for all.

practiceQuestions.hint: The party of the left; a two-word phrase for state-provided support.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Labour won the 1945 election and created the welfare state, including the National Health Service. Priestley's play supports this vision.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each dramatic tradition to the way Priestley uses it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about neat endings, lessons about vices, and 'whodunnit' puzzles.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The well-made play provides the structure of secrets and tension, which Priestley then refuses to resolve. The morality play provides characters embodying vices confronted by a judge-like figure. The detective story provides the investigation, but here everyone is guilty.

pairs.right: Secrets and mounting tension, but the neat ending is deliberately broken
Each character embodies a failing and is confronted by a figure of judgement
An investigation in which every suspect turns out to be guilty

practiceQuestions.text: Put these historical events in chronological order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with the play's setting and end with the London premiere.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The play is set in spring 1912; the Titanic sank in April 1912; the First World War began in 1914; the Second World War ended in 1945; the play opened in London in 1946.
order: The play's setting: an engagement dinner in Brumley
The Titanic sinks on its first voyage
The Second World War ends and Labour wins the election
An Inspector Calls opens in London

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how the position of working-class women in 1912 helps the audience understand Eva Smith's story.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about wages, protection at work, the vote, and what happened to unmarried mothers.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Working-class women in 1912 earned the lowest wages, could be sacked without reason, had no vote and no legal protection from harassment. An unmarried pregnant woman faced disgrace and had to rely on charity. Understanding this shows that Eva's decline from factory to shop to the Palace bar to the charity committee was not bad luck but the predictable result of a system, which is the point Priestley wants the audience to grasp.

markScheme.criterion: Describes the economic vulnerability of working-class women (low wages, easily sacked, few jobs)
Refers to lack of rights or protection (no vote, no legal protection, disgrace for unmarried mothers, reliance on charity)
Explains that this makes Eva's decline seem systemic or predictable rather than accidental, supporting Priestley's message

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best describes how Priestley uses the morality play tradition?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what each Birling represents and what the Inspector does.
practiceQuestions.explanation: As in a morality play, each character embodies a moral failing (Birling greed, Sheila envy, Gerald and Eric lust, Mrs Birling pride) and a figure of judgement confronts them with the consequences.

options.text: Each character embodies a moral failing and the Inspector confronts them like a figure of judgement
The play is set in a medieval castle to remind the audience of old traditions
The Inspector performs a religious ceremony at the end of the play
The play ends with every character forgiven and rewarded

practiceQuestions.text: How does Priestley use Arthur Birling to criticise the values of Edwardian society? Refer to Birling's words and actions and to the historical context.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider his speeches about war and the liner, his attitude to workers and wages, his desire for a knighthood and a business merger, and how the 1945 audience would judge him.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A good answer explains Birling's optimism as typical Edwardian confidence undercut by dramatic irony; his treatment of workers as reflecting the power of employers before the welfare state; his social climbing as showing the rigid class system; his focus on scandal rather than guilt as the older generation's failure; and Priestley's aim of persuading a 1945 audience to reject these values.

markScheme.criterion: Analyses Birling's confident predictions as typical Edwardian optimism undercut by dramatic irony
Explains his treatment of workers or wages in the context of employer power in 1912
Refers to his social climbing (knighthood, marrying into the Crofts) as reflecting the class system
Comments on his concern with scandal or reputation rather than guilt
Explains Priestley's purpose for a 1945 audience

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best explains why Priestley chose the spring of 1912, only weeks before the Titanic sailed and two years before the First World War, as the moment for the Birlings' celebration?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what was about to happen to the confident, comfortable world the Birlings live in.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spring 1912 is the last moment of Edwardian confidence before a series of disasters that the audience knows are coming. Placing the celebration there makes the family's comfort feel fragile and their optimism foolish, and it allows Priestley to use dramatic irony against Birling.

options.text: It is the final moment of Edwardian confidence before disasters the audience knows are coming, so the family's comfort feels fragile
Because women were given the vote in 1912, which is why Sheila is so outspoken
options.feedback: Women did not gain the vote in general elections until 1918 and 1928.

options.text: Because 1912 was the year the welfare state was introduced
options.feedback: The welfare state was built after 1945.

options.text: Because Priestley began writing the play in 1912 and finished it in 1945

practiceQuestions.text: Match each fact about Priestley and the 1940s to the part of the play it helps explain.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the trenches, radio talks about community, the new welfare state, and Priestley's view of the leaders who had failed his generation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Priestley's experience of the trenches lies behind the Inspector's warning of fire, blood and anguish. His wartime broadcasts about building a fairer, more united Britain are echoed in the speech about members of one body. The 1945 welfare state is the answer to Eva's dependence on charity. His belief that the older generation had failed shapes the contrast between the Birlings, who learn nothing, and their children, who change.

pairs.left: Priestley fought in the trenches of the First World War
pairs.right: The Inspector warns of a lesson taught in fire, blood and anguish

pairs.left: Priestley's wartime radio talks called for a fairer, more united Britain
pairs.right: The Inspector's speech that people are members of one body

pairs.left: The 1945 Labour government began building a welfare state
pairs.right: Eva's dependence on a charity committee shows what happens without state support

pairs.left: Priestley believed the older generation's leaders had failed
pairs.right: Mr and Mrs Birling learn nothing while Sheila and Eric change

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about the play's history and setting.

metadata.blanksText: The play was first performed in ___, in the Soviet Union, in 1945. Its London premiere followed in ___. The Birlings belong to the ___ period, named after the king who reigned from 1901 to 1910.

practiceQuestions.hint: The Soviet capital; the year after the war ended; the adjective formed from the name of King Edward VII.
practiceQuestions.explanation: No London theatre was free, so the play was first staged in Moscow in 1945. It opened in London in 1946. The play is set in 1912, near the end of the Edwardian period, a time of confidence for the wealthy and hardship for the poor.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when the play is set, in 1912, no woman in Britain could vote in a general election.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about when the suffragette campaign finally succeeded.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Women could not vote in general elections until 1918, when some women over thirty gained the vote, and full equality came in 1928. This lack of political power is part of why Eva and Edna have so little say in their own lives.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how an audience in 1945 or 1946 might have responded to Birling's confident claims in Act One that there will be no war and that the new liner cannot sink.
practiceQuestions.hint: What did the audience know about the years after 1912? How would that knowledge change their view of Birling, and of the values he stands for?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The audience knew that the liner sank within weeks and that two world wars followed, so Birling's predictions create dramatic irony. This makes him look foolish and arrogant, and discredits everything else he says about business and looking after oneself. Priestley uses the moment to warn the post-war audience not to trust complacent leaders like Birling and to build a different kind of society.

markScheme.criterion: Recognises that the audience knows the predictions were wrong, creating dramatic irony
Explains that this makes Birling look foolish or discredits his views
Links this to Priestley's purpose of encouraging the audience to reject Birling's values and build a better society

practiceQuestions.text:
How does Priestley use Eva Smith and the Inspector to comment on the society of his time? Write about:

- how Eva's story reflects the society of 1912
- how the Inspector's ideas relate to Priestley's own beliefs and to the audience of 1945.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider Eva as a worker and as a woman, the absence of any welfare state, the Inspector as a voice for Priestley's socialism, the wars that lie between 1912 and 1945, and what the audience was deciding about the future.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer shows that Eva's sacking after the strike reflects the lack of rights for workers; that her exploitation and her fate as an unmarried mother reflect the position of women, who had no vote and little protection; that her reliance on charity shows the absence of a welfare state; that the Inspector voices Priestley's socialist belief in community; that his warning of fire, blood and anguish draws on the wars Priestley and his audience had lived through; and that the play was aimed at a 1945 audience choosing a fairer post-war society.

markScheme.criterion: Links Eva's sacking to the lack of rights or security for workers in 1912
Links Eva's exploitation or pregnancy to the position of women in 1912
Explains that her reliance on charity reflects the absence of a welfare state
Presents the Inspector as a voice for Priestley's socialist belief in community
Connects the Inspector's warning to the wars Priestley and his audience had experienced
Relates the play's purpose to the 1945 audience and the choice of a fairer society
